contractSource: Description: "Calculate how many parking stalls fit in a given lot area, or how much space a target number of stalls needs." The form asks for Space Width, Space Length and Aisle Width, and the page notes "90° parking provides maximum capacity but requires wider aisles".
groundTruth: Standard parking-module geometry: each stall occupies (stall width measured along the aisle) × (stall depth perpendicular to the aisle + half the aisle it shares). For 90° stalls the width along the aisle is the stall width and the depth is the stall length. For angle θ: width along aisle = w ÷ sin θ; depth = l·sin θ + w·cos θ.

cases.note: A double-loaded 90° bay that fits an exact count.
cases.derivation: 90 ft × 60 ft lot = 5,400 sq ft. A 60 ft deep bay is one 24 ft aisle with an 18 ft stall row on each side (18 + 24 + 18 = 60). 90 ft of frontage ÷ 9 ft stalls = 10 stalls per side, × 2 sides = 20 stalls. Per stall: 9 × (18 + 24 ÷ 2) = 270 sq ft; 5,400 ÷ 270 = 20. Both methods give 20.

cases.note: The stall and aisle inputs must drive the result.
cases.derivation: Same 5,400 sq ft lot with 8.5 ft × 18 ft stalls and a 24 ft aisle: per stall 8.5 × (18 + 12) = 255 sq ft; 5,400 ÷ 255 = 21.18, so 21 whole stalls. Narrower stalls must fit more cars than the 20 of the 9 ft case.

cases.note: Angled stalls use more area per car than 90°, so the same lot holds fewer.
cases.derivation: 45°, 9 × 18 ft stalls, 13 ft one-way aisle. Width along the aisle = 9 ÷ sin 45° = 12.73 ft. Depth = 18·sin 45° + 9·cos 45° = 12.73 + 6.36 = 19.09 ft. Per stall = 12.73 × (19.09 + 13 ÷ 2) = 12.73 × 25.59 = 325.7 sq ft. 5,400 ÷ 325.7 = 16.6, so about 16 stalls (±1 for layout rounding) — fewer than the 20 at 90°.
